endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: Conversely, GenAI should be restricted or disabled for message categories that are inherently high-risk: chest pain equivalents, neurologic symptoms, pregnancy-related bleeding, mental health crisis language, anticoagulant complications, pediatrics with limited history, or situations where missing one sentence can change urgency.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether assigning portal messages to risk tiers changes the safety of AI-drafted replies, and no study documents the hazard directly. The recommendation rests on a single commentary that advises restricting or disabling AI drafting for message categories it judges high-risk.

perspectives.view: The evidence base consists of one commentary using "should" language and zero studies of the practice or the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion without supporting data cannot establish certainty of effect. The tiering thresholds, the categories assigned to each tier, and the clinician actions tied to them have not been evaluated for accuracy or outcomes.

The endorsing commentary names categories such as chest pain equivalents, neurologic symptoms, pregnancy-related bleeding, mental health crisis language, and anticoagulant complications as candidates for restriction. These choices reflect where missed urgency may cause severe harm. No supplied study reports how often a tiering rule misclassifies an urgent message into a lower tier and allows a draft to proceed.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how accurately a risk-tiering method sorts real portal messages, how often high-risk messages are misrouted to AI drafting, and whether tiering changes clinician review behavior, reply errors, response times, and downstream patient harm compared with untiered drafting.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Messages written in other languages or in nonstandard phrasing may be classified differently by a tiering rule, and without testing in these groups a health system cannot know whether urgent messages from these patients are sorted as reliably as others.
